Playtime–wellbeing associations are practically null and vary little across video game genres

Abstract

Video game research often treats games as a monolithic category, and single-game or single-platform studies leave open whether findings generalise across the medium. In this Registered Report, we used digital trace data from the Open Play dataset to test whether (H1) total playtime is meaningfully associated with mental wellbeing and (H2) this association differs by game genre. The data comprise 226,000 hours of playtime across 4,152 games from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam for 1,608 UK and US adults, linked to genre metadata and 6,293 biweekly wellbeing assessments (SWEMWBS). Judged against a preregistered threshold for practical significance, neither within-person fluctuations nor habitual differences in total playtime were meaningfully linked to wellbeing. The preregistered joint test found within-person differences between genres under our multi-genre attribution but not under the preregistered single-genre attribution, and no between-person differences. Under an exploratory hierarchical model, the estimated spread of the within-person genre effects implied that fewer than one of the 14 genres was expected to lie more than 0.06 points per hour from the average genre effect, and a multi-membership model estimated the spread less precisely. An exploratory daily-timescale analysis gave the same picture for total playtime and the hierarchical model’s genre spread. Genre differences appear to be the wrong place to look for gaming’s wellbeing effects, as genre labels are too coarse a proxy for the psychological experiences that plausibly drive them. We therefore regard finer-grained characterisations of play as the more promising avenue for further study.

Introduction

Identifying how different types of games and gameplay affect wellbeing is vital in light of the contrast between popular sentiment, which treats video games as a harm to those who play them in the latest of a long line of technology panics (Orben, 2020), and empirical evidence that playtime in general is not a meaningful predictor of wellbeing, using data from both specific games (Larrieu et al., 2023) and platforms (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025). A common objection to these null findings is that the effect of play must depend on which games people play. Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain why aggregate playtime is poorly predictive of wellbeing, including displacement of beneficial activities, satisfaction or frustration of basic psychological needs, and selection effects whereby individuals with lower wellbeing play more (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025). Displacement aside, these mechanisms operate at the level of game features or player experience rather than at the level of total time spent; playtime might be, at best, a moderator (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025). In causal terms, playing is a compound exposure that comes in many versions, so an average association across all of them answers an ambiguous question (Magnusson et al., 2024).

Given the vast heterogeneity between games, our understanding of the psychological processes and outcomes of digital play has been limited by video game effects research’s widespread use of either undifferentiated self-report data, or digital trace data focusing on a single game or a handful of games (Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Brühlmann et al., 2020; Johannes et al., 2021; Larrieu et al., 2023; Vuorre et al., 2022; Vuorre, Ballou, et al., 2024). While understandable given the limited resources and lack of objective data available to independent researchers, this narrow scope has left the field guessing whether identified relationships are unique to the studied titles or whether they apply universally across games. One step forward is therefore to capture comprehensive play behaviour data across the varied games and gaming platforms users regularly engage in, and to differentiate games using structured taxonomies. The most widespread system for classifying games is game genres, albeit not without some controversy (Clarke et al., 2017; Starosta et al., 2024; Vargas-Iglesias, 2020).

Game Genres and Wellbeing

Consistent null findings for the effects of playtime on wellbeing have generated calls for the unpacking of raw decontextualised playtime into more informative measures that consider games’ varied characteristics and affordances (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024). Game genres offer a structured way to differentiate between video games and their corresponding play experiences (Starosta et al., 2024). Genre differences in player behaviour, cognition, and gaming disorder symptoms are often proposed (André et al., 2024; Dobrowolski et al., 2015; Hazel et al., 2022; Raith et al., 2021): for example, action games have been linked to increased visual attention (Palaus et al., 2017), cognitive and attentional control (Anguera et al., 2013; Bavelier & Green, 2019), and working memory (Blacker et al., 2014). Massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs), first-person shooters, real-time strategy games (RTS), and Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games have been associated with higher gaming disorder symptoms (Elliott et al., 2012; King et al., 2019; Na et al., 2017; Rehbein et al., 2021). Player experience also differs by genre: MOBA players report less immersion and autonomy and more frustration than players of single-player genres (Johnson et al., 2015), and role-playing games are the genre players most often perceive as beneficial (Hazel et al., 2022). Randomised controlled trials with casual games and exergames induced positive moods and reduced stress (Huang et al., 2017; Russoniello et al., 2009). These findings suggest that the effects of video games are not uniform and that genre differences exist in both gaming behaviour and its impact on wellbeing. This evidence is, however, between-person: the observational studies compare people who favour different genres, and the trials assign people to one genre for a short period, so to our knowledge no study has asked whether a person’s wellbeing rises and falls with their own genre playtime over time.

With more than 10,000 new games released each year (Notis, 2021), an accessible classification system is essential for studying and comparing video games at scale. Genres, while defined by convention and neither exclusive nor exhaustive as labels (Clarke et al., 2017; Starosta et al., 2024; Vargas-Iglesias, 2020), remain the most pragmatic means of categorising video games. Psychologists have differentiated games based on genre for decades (Griffiths, 1993; Wolf, 2002), but must negotiate challenges in definition, overlaps between genres, and the continuous evolution of genres as new games are released. The overlaps are not a marginal problem: in metadata databases such as IGDB, most of the games people play carry more than one genre label (see Methods), which complicates any analysis that files each game under a single genre. Genre labels conflate distinct facets of games, such as gameplay style, purpose, and mood (Lee et al., 2014), and factor-analytic decompositions of crowd-sourced game tags produce genre structures that diverge from conventional labels (Li, 2020). Even the cognitive literature that produced the best-known genre-specific claims now treats genre labels as a weak proxy for the mechanics that matter, because games increasingly blend mechanics across genres, as popular titles such as Skyrim do (Bavelier & Green, 2019). Genres are therefore best treated not as definitive taxonomical statements but as crude yet practical tools for organising a growing and diversifying library.

There is a lack of consistent standardisation of game genres, leading to inconsistent classification of video game genres across psychological research (Starosta et al., 2024). Starosta et al. (2024) counted 46 distinct taxonomies across the 96 articles they examined; only 50 articles (52%) drew on an existing or combined source for their classification, and 18 (19%) did not specify how their categories were constructed at all. Genre classifications are typically self-reported by participants or assigned by authors, and the same games are habitually classified into different genres across studies. This subjectivity undermines the validity of existing self-report or researcher-ascribed genre taxonomies for the meaningful comparison of results across studies.

Structured, crowd-sourced metadata repositories such as SteamDB, The Games Database, and the Internet Games Database (IGDB) offer a more reliable alternative, involving both game developers and large player samples in collaboratively maintaining genre labels (Lee et al., 2015; Li & Zhang, 2020; Starosta et al., 2024). Within the constraints of genre as a means of categorising games, metadata repositories best accommodate the fluidity of genres over time (Cohen, 1986) and enable comparative research at scale.

The Present Study

In line with prior evidence (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Larrieu et al., 2023), our first hypothesis predicts the absence of a meaningful relationship between playtime and wellbeing, now with digital trace data across several platforms and thousands of games:

H1. Total cross-platform playtime is not meaningfully associated with fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (H1a, “within-person”) or with average wellbeing over the full study period (H1b, “between-person”).

In practical terms, with H1a we ask whether a participant’s wellbeing in a given two-week wave deviates from their own average when their playtime in that wave does, and with H1b whether participants who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than those who play less. Fluctuations in H1 therefore refer to deviations from a person’s own average rather than to changes between consecutive waves. What counts as a meaningful association is fixed in advance by the smallest effect size of interest defined in the Methods.

Second, following previous literature (André et al., 2024; Dobrowolski et al., 2015; Elliott et al., 2012; Hazel et al., 2022; Raith et al., 2021; Rehbein et al., 2021), we predict that genres vary in their relation to wellbeing, with some potentially positive and others potentially negative, varying in strength. Put more formally:

H2. Genres differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (H2a, “within-person”) and to average wellbeing over the full study period (H2b, “between-person”).

With H2a we ask: when a participant plays more than their own average this wave, does it matter what genres that extra playtime is in? With H2b we ask the between-person complement: among people who play more overall, does it matter whether that habitual extra playtime is concentrated in, for example, RPGs versus Shooters versus other genres? By examining heterogeneity across genres (Vuorre, Kay, et al., 2024), we thus test with H2 whether it is justified to generalise video game effects across genres, the generalisability that single-title studies sometimes assume (Yarkoni, 2022).

Beyond the preregistered hypotheses, we report one exploratory extension that was not preregistered. The biweekly window comprises potentially many individual play sessions and a single retrospective wellbeing judgement, so the preregistered tests leave open whether associations operate on shorter timescales. As such, we re-examine both hypotheses at the daily level.

Methods

Data Source and Participants

The analyses reported here are part of a Stage 1 Registered Report (Ballou, Földes, et al., 2024), and the data collected for this study are part of the Open Play dataset (Ballou, Földes, Vuorre, et al., 2025, v1.2.6), a longitudinal dataset that combined multi-platform video game digital trace data with daily and biweekly psychological measures from adult gamers in the UK and US over a three-month period. Qualifying participants completed the intake survey between Sep 2024 and Jun 2025. The digital trace data span the following periods: Nintendo (May 2022 to Oct 2025), Xbox (May 2022 to Sep 2025), Steam (Nov 2024 to Oct 2025), iOS (Mar 2025 to Aug 2025), Android (Mar 2025 to Aug 2025).

This study received ethical approval from the Social Sciences and Humanities Inter-Divisional Research Ethics Committee at the University of Oxford (OII_CIA_23_107). All participants provided informed consent at the start of the study, including consent to their data being shared openly for reanalysis.

Participants were paid at an average rate of £12/hour, equating to £0.20 for a 1-minute screening, £2 for the 10-minute intake survey (plus £5 for linking at least one account with recent data), £0.80 for each 4-minute daily survey, and £2 for each 10-minute biweekly survey. Participants received a £10 bonus payment for completing at least 24 out of 30 daily surveys and/or 5 out of 6 biweekly surveys.

Of the 33,046 participants who completed the intake survey, 2,238 met the preregistered screening and linking criteria. The analytic sample comprises the 1,608 qualified participants who provided valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly survey wave. This definition corrects the sample of our first analyses: a later Open Play release (v1.2.4) corrected false positives in the qualification flag, revoking it for participants whose intake had not passed the screening and linking checks, and we excluded them (133 participants of the earlier analytic sample), together with 97 participants whose biweekly responses carry a participant identifier that matches no intake record, an identifier mismatch in the data provider’s survey export (Appendix A, Deviation D7; Table 5 in Appendix D compares the preregistered estimates with and without them). We measured playtime for these participants from their linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam accounts. Rather than excluding participants and waves without recorded play on these platforms, we retained them with zero hours: 81 participants (5%) had no recorded play in any wave, and 897 of the 6,293 person-waves (14%) had none in that wave. In the full analytic sample, 1,520 participants (95%) had at least one session of a game that we could match to a genre. All 1,608 analytic-sample participants have an age within the 18-40 screening range (912 US, 696 UK; mean age 27.1 years, 65% men), so the demographic sensitivity analysis starts from the full analytic sample. We report full demographic characteristics, including country-level breakdowns, in Table 3.

Measures

Figure 1 shows the distributions and structure of the key variables.

Wellbeing. We assessed wellbeing with the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (SWEMWBS) (Tennant et al., 2007), a 7-item short form of the WEMWBS covering psychological functioning and subjective wellbeing over the past 2 weeks, with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from “None of the time” to “All of the time.” We score the scale as the arithmetic mean of the 7 items (range: 1–5). Internal consistency across all analytic person-waves was high (McDonald’s ωt = 0.89, Cronbach’s α = 0.89). We define all reported coefficients, the priors, and the preregistered SESOI on this item-mean scale.

Video game playtime. Digital trace data from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam provide session-level records (per-title start and end timestamps), while iOS and Android contribute only daily aggregate minutes (no game-level metadata). Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam therefore contribute to both H1 (total playtime) and H2 (genre-specific playtime); iOS and Android enter only the first positive control, which compares self-reported with logged playtime, and the preregistered all-platform H1 model, which Appendix D reports with the other preregistered frequentist analyses (Table 5; Appendix A, Deviation D4). Our findings therefore concern play on Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam and do not speak to mobile play.

Game genre classification. We obtained genre labels for Nintendo and Steam games by cross-referencing the game titles in the digital trace data with the Internet Games Database (IGDB). IGDB is, to our knowledge, the only database with complete multi-platform metadata coverage that offers an API for programmatic data retrieval. IGDB crowd-sources its genre labels from a predefined list of options: community members submit contributions (e.g., a new game or an alternative categorisation), which administrators and moderators vet before they appear in the database; IGDB documents its contribution guidelines publicly, including how it holds submissions for review and the predefined list of genres (https://github.com/twitchtv/igdb-contribution-guidelines/wiki). We could not match Xbox titles to IGDB, because Xbox provided us only with anonymised title identifiers; instead, we took the genre labels that Xbox supplies for each title through its store and mapped those onto the IGDB taxonomy. In total, we collected 23 distinct raw IGDB genre labels, converted the Xbox store genres into the IGDB taxonomy, and collapsed them into 14 genre categories (e.g., Strategy subsumes Turn-Based Strategy (TBS), Real-Time Strategy (RTS), Tactical, and MOBA; Puzzle subsumes Card & Board Game and Quiz/Trivia). Appendix B gives the complete mapping table, including where the implemented collapsing departs from the preregistered one (Deviation D2), and Appendix C the descriptive statistics by genre. We did not consider IGDB “themes” or other metadata fields. Overall, we matched 94% of in-study playtime to at least one study genre (Steam 96.2%, Nintendo 92.1%, Xbox 79.7%); unmatched playtime counts towards total playtime but towards no genre.

Genre co-occurrence and compositional multi-genre attribution. Across the 3,676 individual games in our dataset, 62% carry more than one genre label, leading to 324 distinct genre combinations. Figure 2 shows the playtime-weighted co-occurrence structure across the 40 most-played combinations, which together account for 88% of all genre-matched playtime, and Table 1 lists the ten most-played combinations with their top titles. Because a majority of games carry several labels, the rule that turns a session of a multi-genre game into genre exposure variables decides what a genre coefficient means, so we set out the four rules we considered and the choices we made before describing the models. The preregistration specified the first; the confirmatory model M2 and the exploratory model M3 use the third (Appendix A, Deviation D1); and the exploratory model M4 uses the fourth.

Primary attribution, the preregistered rule, assigns each game to the genre that IGDB lists first and counts a session’s full duration towards that genre alone. A 60-minute session of Skyrim (Adventure and RPG) would count as 60 minutes of whichever of its two genres IGDB happens to list first and nothing towards the other. Genre exposures then stay mutually exclusive and sum to total playtime, but the rule discards the second and third labels of most games and makes the exposure depend on the order in which IGDB lists them. After data access and before any results were known, we decided not to use it (Deviation D1).

Partial attribution splits a session’s playtime across its genres. A 60-minute session of Skyrim (Adventure and RPG) would contribute 30 minutes to Adventure and 30 minutes to RPG (or potentially a different, unequal partition). Exposures then still sum to total playtime, but the rule penalises multi-genre games: each additional label a game carries lowers its contribution to every genre, although the game belongs fully to each of its genres rather than partially. We rejected this rule for that reason.

Full attribution, which we used for M2 and M3, counts a session’s full duration towards every genre it carries. The same 60-minute Skyrim session counts as 60 minutes of Adventure and 60 minutes of RPG. Consider a person who plays 60 minutes of Skyrim (Adventure + RPG) and 60 minutes of Final Fantasy XIV Online (RPG only). Under partial attribution, Skyrim contributes 30 minutes to each genre, yielding 30 total minutes of Adventure and 90 minutes of RPG, a 1:3 ratio implying three times as much RPG engagement as Adventure. Under full attribution, Skyrim contributes 60 minutes to each genre, yielding 60 minutes of Adventure and 120 minutes of RPG, a 2:1 ratio that better reflects that RPG-labelled content received twice the engagement of Adventure-labelled content. A consequence is that genre exposures no longer sum to total playtime. Genre-level coefficients therefore represent the association with an added hour of that genre’s exposure holding total playtime constant, for example, replacing a single-genre RPG session with a dual-genre Adventure/RPG session of the same length.

Proportional multi-membership weighting, which we used for M4, converts the full-attribution hours into compositional weights by dividing each genre’s exposure hours by total exposure (e.g., 33.3% Adventure, 66.7% RPG for a wave consisting of 60 minutes of Skyrim and 60 minutes of Final Fantasy XIV Online) and uses these as the weights of a multiple-membership structure (Cafri et al., 2015; Fielding & Goldstein, 2006) on a single total-playtime slope. Genre does not enter M4 as an independent predictor of wellbeing but as a modifier of the playtime–wellbeing slope: a wave consisting mostly of RPG play has its playtime coefficient adjusted mostly by the RPG slope adjustment, with other genres contributing in proportion to their share of that wave’s play. M4 draws the genre-specific slope adjustments from a common distribution, and the standard deviation of that distribution, σs, describes the genre differences that H2 concerns. This weighting shares a limitation with partial attribution, because adding a genre label to a game lowers the shares of the labels it already carries, so none of the four rules is free of trade-offs. In sum, M2 and M3 model full-attribution exposures, M4 models the same hours as proportional weights, and no model in the main text uses the preregistered primary attribution (Appendix D reports the preregistered tests under it), so every genre coefficient below describes exposure to games carrying a label rather than to games filed under it.

Demographics. Participants self-reported age, gender, ethnicity, country, and employment at baseline. Table 3 in Appendix C reports full demographic characteristics.

Analytic Approach

We conducted all analyses in R (R Core Team, 2025) and wrote the manuscript in Quarto (Allaire et al., 2025). We fit four Bayesian multilevel models with brms (Bürkner, 2017) at the biweekly timescale, and refit each at the daily timescale as an exploratory extension. We preregistered two of them: the model of total playtime (M1) tests H1, and the genre model with independently estimated genre coefficients (M2) tests H2. We added the other two after seeing the M2 results, to examine their robustness: M3 keeps M2’s predictors but pools the genre coefficients through a common prior, whereas M4 keeps total playtime as the single predictor, as in M1, and lets each wave’s genre composition modify its slope; both describe the size of the genre differences through the estimated spread of the genre effects, and M4 also yields H1 estimates. All four models use the brms default priors, and Appendix F gives their equations and priors in full. We organise the results by hypothesis and describe the preregistered models first and the exploratory models second, and we label every figure row, legend entry, and table row by model, with its preregistration status. We catalogue deviations from the preregistered plan in Appendix A and flag them below where they affect interpretation, and we report the preregistered frequentist analyses in full in Appendix D.

Smallest Effect Size of Interest

Establishing the absence of a practically significant effect requires committing in advance to a threshold below which an association is too small to matter, the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). By practically significant, we mean the smallest change in wellbeing that a player would themselves notice, known also as a minimally important difference (MID). Following previous studies, we set the MID at 0.3 points on the SWEMWBS item-mean scale (1–5; equivalent to 2.1 points on the 7–35 summed scale), converging with anchor- and distribution-based estimates of the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (WEMWBS) (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Maheswaran et al., 2012) and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) (Anvari & Lakens, 2021).

To calculate the SESOI, we also need to know how large a change in playtime is realistically available to reach the MID. Because US adults average approximately 5 hours of daily leisure time (Sturm & Cohen, 2019), the figure to which we anchored the preregistered SESOI, we take 5 hours as an upper bound on how much daily play could plausibly rise or fall without displacing other behaviours that arguably impact wellbeing more than play (e.g., sleep). More recent diaries put the figure lower for our age range. Americans aged 23 to 38 averaged about 4.3 hours a day in 2019 (Freeman, 2022), and 3.8 to 4.7 hours by age band between 20 and 44 in 2024 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025); UK adults aged 18 to 44 averaged between 4.3 and 5.2 hours in 2014, depending on sex and age band (summing the leisure components in Table 3 of García Román & Gracia (2022)). Five hours is therefore an upper bound, and the preregistered SESOI the stricter of the two choices. Our SESOI is the ratio of the two: 0.3 ÷ 5 = 0.06 points per hour, the same threshold used by Ballou, Sewall, et al. (2024). An association smaller than 0.06 points per hour means that even a person who shifted their entire 5-hour daily leisure budget into or out of gaming would not experience a noticeable change in wellbeing.

We evaluate the individual coefficients, the two total-playtime coefficients of H1 and each genre’s within-person and between-person coefficients, against the interval between the negative and positive SESOI [−0.06, +0.06], also known as the Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE) (Kruschke, 2018). If a coefficient’s 95% credible interval (CI) falls entirely inside the ROPE, we consider the effect practically null, meaning even the largest plausible effect is too small to matter; a CI entirely beyond either bound indicates a practically positive or negative effect, and one straddling either edge is inconclusive. Throughout, CI denotes a 95% credible interval from a Bayesian model; the preregistered frequentist tests in Appendix D use 90% confidence intervals, as the equivalence test requires, and are labelled as such, so the interval level identifies the type. This rule replaces the preregistered decision grid for H1 (Deviation D3), which classifies the 90% confidence interval of each H1 coefficient as follows: an interval entirely beyond either bound indicates a practically significant positive or negative association; one that excludes zero and crosses a bound, a positive or negative association that may be practically significant; one that excludes zero and lies inside the bounds, a positive or negative association that is not practically significant; one that covers zero and lies inside the bounds, no practically significant association; and one that covers zero and crosses a bound, an inconclusive result. Appendix D reports the preregistered analyses under this grid.

We test H2 with the preregistered joint Wald tests of whether the genre coefficients are equal, which we run separately for the 14 within-person (H2a) and the 14 between-person (H2b) coefficients on a maximum-likelihood fit of M2 with the same fixed effects and random intercept. These tests answer H2, and we report them at the start of the H2 results. A rejection shows that at least two genres differ but not by how much, and the preregistration fixed no threshold for the size of differences between genres. We therefore describe the size of the differences without converting it into a verdict. For each model we compute the spread s of the genre effects at each posterior draw: as the standard deviation of M2’s 14 independently estimated coefficients (which includes their estimation error and can therefore overstate the spread), as τgenre in M3, and as σs in M4. Treating the genre effects as normally distributed around their average, we translate s into three quantities and summarise each in the text by its posterior mean and 95% CI; tables and the daily section report posterior means. The first is the share of genres whose effect lies more than 0.06 from the average genre effect, 2[1 - \Phi(0.06/s)], where \Phi is the standard normal distribution function, together with the expected number of our 14 genres that this share implies. The second is the share of genre pairs whose effects differ by more than 0.06, 2[1 - \Phi(0.06/(\sqrt{2}\,s))], because the difference between two genre effects drawn from the same distribution has standard deviation \sqrt{2}\,s. The third is the share of the genre-effect distribution, a normal distribution with the model’s average genre effect as its mean and s as its standard deviation, that lies outside the ROPE (Vuorre, Kay, et al., 2024). Unlike the first two, this share depends on the average genre effect as well as on the spread, so it describes whether the associations are practically null in every genre rather than whether genres differ. We do not turn these quantities into a verdict, because we can translate the SESOI into a threshold for differences between genres in more than one defensible way, and the translations set different thresholds: for 95% of genre effects to lie within 0.06 of the average, the spread must be below 0.031 (0.06 ÷ 1.96), whereas for 95% of genre pairs to differ by less than 0.06, it must be below 0.022 (0.06 ÷ (1.96 × √2)). We report both values as reference points only.

Preregistered Models

M1: Total Playtime

M1 is the preregistered model for H1: is total playtime across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam associated with wellbeing? We split each participant’s playtime into a between-person part, their mean across waves (including the 35 waves with an incomplete SWEMWBS, which do not enter the models), and a within-person part, each wave’s deviation from that mean, and regress SWEMWBS on both, so the model returns two coefficients: \beta_W, the association between a wave’s deviation from a person’s usual playtime and that wave’s wellbeing, and \beta_B, the association between a person’s habitual playtime and their average wellbeing. We estimate a random intercept for each participant because people differ in baseline wellbeing, and a random slope for within-person playtime because the association need not be identical for everyone (equations and priors in Appendix F).

M2: Independent Genre Coefficients

M2 is the preregistered specification for H2. We estimate a separate within-person and between-person coefficient for each of the 14 genres, independently of one another, with a random intercept per participant. Because genre exposures are non-exclusive, their sum does not recover total playtime, and M2 therefore contains no separate total-playtime term. We departed from the preregistered specification in two respects. First, a game’s full playtime counts towards every one of its genre labels (Deviation D1), whereas the preregistration assigned each game its first IGDB genre only; this adds no coefficients for genre combinations, since there is still one coefficient per genre and dimension, but the 14 exposure columns overlap. Second, the preregistration specified per-participant random slopes for the within-person genre terms, with all random-effect correlations fixed at zero. When we fitted this structure by maximum likelihood to M2’s data, it was singular, with most of the 14 slope standard deviations estimated at zero, as the preregistration anticipated, so we retained the random intercept only (equations and priors in Appendix F).

Exploratory Models

We did not preregister the models in this section and report them as exploratory throughout, together with the daily-timescale refits described at the end of this section.

M3: Hierarchical Prior

For M3 we keep M2’s predictors and random intercept but use a multilevel model that treats the 14 genre-specific coefficients as draws from a common normal distribution rather than as unrelated quantities, and we estimate both the centre and the standard deviation of that distribution, separately for the within-person and between-person dimensions. The centres, γW and γB, are the common genre effects, the average association of genre playtime with wellbeing around which the genre-specific coefficients vary. The standard deviations, τgenre (τwithin and τbetween), measure how widely the genre coefficients spread around these common effects, which is the heterogeneity H2 targets. In the Results we report the common genre effects beside the mean of the 14 independently estimated M2 coefficients, their unpooled counterpart. The shared distribution also produces partial pooling: it pulls the estimates for rarely played genres towards the common genre effect, whereas genres with ample data retain estimates close to their independent values. Per-genre intervals from M3 therefore partly reflect the data on the other genres. An earlier version of M3 fixed the centres of these distributions at zero; following co-author review, and after the results of that version were known, we estimate them instead, so that τ measures the spread around the common genre effect rather than around zero. Because sampling near τ = 0 is numerically difficult, we estimate M3 in a non-centred form that is mathematically equivalent to sampling each coefficient directly, use conservative sampler settings, and report divergence counts and R-hat diagnostics for every model alongside the results (equations and priors in Appendix F).

M4: Multi-Membership

M4 describes each wave by its total playtime and by the genre composition of that playtime, the representation that panel D of Figure 1 uses for days. The model keeps total playtime as the predictor and inherits M1’s structure, including the overall \beta_W and \beta_B, and lets the composition of that playtime modify the playtime slope. Each genre adjusts a wave’s slope in proportion to its share of the wave’s genre exposure, so a wave consisting mostly of Shooter play is governed mostly by the Shooter slope adjustment, and a wave divided between Adventure and RPG draws on both adjustments in proportion. As described under the attribution rules, M4 draws the genre adjustments from a common distribution whose standard deviation, σs (within and between persons), quantifies how much the playtime–wellbeing slope varies with the genres being played (equations, priors, and a parameter-recovery check in Appendix F).

Daily Timescale

To assess whether our findings hold on a shorter timescale, we conducted an exploratory daily-timescale analysis, whose plan we fixed after the preregistered analyses were complete but before we estimated any daily model. We made two changes after the daily results were known: we estimated M3-D’s centres as in M3, and we gave all daily models the brms default priors (Appendix F) instead of the plan’s priors, which had rescaled the biweekly priors to the life-satisfaction slider. The Open Play study asked US participants to complete daily surveys for the first 30 study days, including a life-satisfaction item (“I was satisfied with my life today”) answered on a 0–100 slider (Ballou, Földes, Vuorre, et al., 2025), which serves as the outcome. The exposure is console and PC playtime from 4:00 a.m. local time of the response’s waking day up to the survey completion timestamp, which we computed from the same session-level telemetry. Of the 14,384 diary responses from 888 participants in the analytic sample, we analysed the 13,071 responses (90.9%), from 726 participants, for which telemetry and an analysable same-day window were available. We again split playtime into a within-person and a between-person part, but measure the two parts over different windows. The within-person part is the difference between the day’s same-day playtime and the participant’s own average same-day playtime. The between-person part is the participant’s habitual playtime over a full day, so that differences between participants remain expressed in the same daily-hour units as in the biweekly analysis. We construct the SESOI for the slider in the same way as the preregistered one, as a minimally important difference divided by the roughly five hours of daily leisure realistically available (Sturm & Cohen, 2019). No anchor-based minimally important difference exists for a single-item life-satisfaction slider, so we set it at 5 slider points, a deliberately conservative choice. It lies below two available benchmarks, half the within-person SD of the slider (6 points) and the preregistered minimally important difference expressed as a share of its scale range (7.5% of 0–100, or 7.5 points), and a smaller minimally important difference makes practical equivalence harder to claim rather than easier. Dividing by five hours gives 1 slider point per hour of daily play. We refit the model specifications (M1–M4) at the daily level and label them M1-D to M4-D. They use the same brms default priors as the biweekly models, so brms sets the intercept location and the standard-deviation scales from the life-satisfaction outcome: the intercept prior is centred at its median, and the scale of the intercept prior and of every standard-deviation prior, including τ in M3-D, is the larger of 2.5 and its median absolute deviation. Appendix D details window construction, sample exclusions, and four robustness refits.

Missing Data

Missingness in the outcome takes two forms. Item-level missingness is rare and all-or-nothing, with 35 submitted surveys missing all seven SWEMWBS items. Wave nonresponse is the dominant form of missingness, survey completion declined from 100% at wave 1 to 45% at wave 6, leaving 3,355 of the 9,648 person-waves (34.8%) without an observed SWEMWBS. The dataset paper documents retention over the study period and missingness by data source (Ballou, Földes, Vuorre, et al., 2025).

We fit the models to the observed outcomes, an approach that is valid provided outcome missingness is at random given the modelled covariates and random effects. To test that assumption, we multiply imputed SWEMWBS on the complete participant × wave grid with two-level multiple imputation by chained equations (mice and miceadds) (Robitzsch & Grund, 2024; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011): predictive mean matching (2l.pmm) with participants as random-intercept clusters (van Buuren, 2018), and m = 100 imputations, a number we set from the pilot fraction of missing information by von Hippel’s (2020) two-stage rule. Predictive mean matching donates observed values, so imputed scores respect the 1–5 scale. We fitted frequentist counterparts of the analysis models to each imputed dataset and pooled the estimates by Rubin’s rules; neither pooled H1 coefficient was practically significant, as in the complete-case analyses, whereas the pooled tests no longer reject equality of the within-person genre coefficients (Appendix D, Table 8); ?@tbl-frequentist-Registered Reports the preregistered complete-case tests. We did not impute playtime because tracking was continuous and automatic even for participants with missing survey waves, so within linked platforms an absence of play is recorded absence rather than missing data, and exposures exist for every person-wave.

Results

The analytic sample comprised 1,608 participants with a valid SWEMWBS response in at least one biweekly wave, yielding 6,293 person-wave observations (M = 3.9 of 6 waves per participant; see Missing Data). We measured playtime from linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam telemetry; participants played an average of 1.78 hours per day (SD = 2.02) across the three platforms.

We report the preregistered data quality controls first and then each hypothesis in turn. Within each hypothesis section, the preregistered model (M1 for H1, M2 for H2) comes first and the exploratory models (M4 for H1; M3 and M4 for H2) second, and figure rows, legend entries, and table rows are labelled by model and preregistration status. The exploratory daily-timescale refits and the robustness checks close the section.

Data Quality Controls

Before testing the hypotheses, we ran the three preregistered positive controls, each of which checks that the data reproduce a pattern known to hold.

First, self-reported biweekly playtime correlated positively with digital trace playtime (r = 0.483, 95% confidence interval [0.461, 0.505], p < .001).

Second, session integrity largely held. Xbox contained 0 overlapping sessions, and no Steam session’s recorded playtime exceeded its elapsed wall-clock duration (0 violations). Nintendo retained a small number of overlapping sessions: 675 of 288,082 sessions (0.23%), with a median overlap of 9.8 minutes and accounting for 0.09% of total Nintendo playtime.

All overlapping sessions could be traced to concurrent use of multiple consoles linked to one account (e.g., a Switch Lite overlapping an OLED model). Given their rarity, we judged them neither a sign of systematic data quality problems nor frequent enough to affect the estimates.

Third, men played more shooter games than women (M = 0.538 vs. 0.337 hrs/day, t(997.6) = 4.37, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.23), meeting the preregistered criterion of a significant difference in the expected direction and consistent with population studies of gendered genre preferences (Rehbein et al., 2016). All three controls passed, and we proceeded to the hypothesis tests.

  # brms default priors (since 2026-10-13; Methods): flat on b,
  # Student-t(3, median(y), 2.5) on the Intercept, half-Student-t(3, 0, 2.5)
  # on sigma and the SDs, LKJ(1) on the correlation.
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h1_rewb_model")

Code 
# M3: same genre-exposure structure as M2, but the 14 within-person and the 14
# between-person genre coefficients are drawn from common normal
# distributions: beta_W,g ~ Normal(gamma_W, tau_within) and
# beta_B,g ~ Normal(gamma_B, tau_between), with the centres gamma and the
# spreads tau estimated. No total_within/total_between: genre exposure columns
# are non-exclusive (full attribution), so partialing out total playtime would
# leave only multi-genre inflation artifacts.
#
# Non-centred form (since 2026-10-14). Writing beta_g = gamma + r_g with
# r_g ~ Normal(0, tau) gives sum_g x_g beta_g = gamma * sum_g x_g +
# sum_g x_g r_g: a fixed slope on the summed exposure plus a multi-membership
# intercept over the 14 genres whose weights are the exposures. brms samples
# group-level effects as r = tau * z with z ~ Normal(0, 1), so this is the
# non-centred parameterisation of the same model (same likelihood; same flat
# prior on gamma and half-Student-t(3, 0, S) prior on tau). Every parameter
# keeps its brms default, so no prior and no stanvars are set: gamma_W =
# b_sum_within and gamma_B = b_sum_between are flat; tau_within and
# tau_between are the SDs of the two mm intercepts (default sd prior,
# half-Student-t(3, 0, S), S = max(2.5, mad(y)) = 2.5 for SWEMWBS). The only
# difference from the centred fit concerns the default Intercept prior: brms
# centres the population-level predictors before placing the default
# Intercept prior, so that prior now sits on the expected outcome at the mean
# summed exposures with every genre deviation at zero (a Student-t with scale
# 2.5, wide relative to any genre contribution).
# scale = FALSE is essential: the weights are exposures in hours/day (the
# within-person ones signed), not shares, and must enter unrescaled.
# Per-genre coefficients for every downstream use: beta_g = gamma + r_g,
# computed draw-wise (h2_hier_nc below), as for M4's genre slopes.
# History: models/h2_hier_model_v2 had the centres fixed at zero (stanvars);
# models/h2_hier_model_v3 (2026-10-13) estimated the centres, but in the
# centred form (stanvars + 28 structural normal(mu, tau) priors) it had 68
# divergent transitions in 16,000 draws at adapt_delta = 0.999 (Neal's funnel
# as tau approaches zero; archived fit kept for comparison);
# models/h2_hier_model_v4 is this non-centred multi-membership form
# (2026-10-14). New file names keep an older fit from being reloaded through
# brms `file =` (scripts/refit_v126.sh).
h2_hier_data <- analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs))
hier_genres  <- sub("^gh_", "", gh_vars)  # 14 genre slugs, alphabetical
stopifnot(length(hier_genres) == 14, !anyDuplicated(hier_genres),
          identical(gh_within,  paste0(gh_vars, "_within")),
          identical(gh_between, paste0(gh_vars, "_between")))
# 2 x 14 constant genre-label columns, one per membership slot; level k of
# the k-th column is the k-th genre, so each mm term has exactly 14 levels.
hier_gw_cols <- paste0("gW_", seq_along(hier_genres))
hier_gb_cols <- paste0("gB_", seq_along(hier_genres))
for (k in seq_along(hier_genres)) {
  h2_hier_data[[hier_gw_cols[k]]] <- factor(hier_genres[k], levels = hier_genres)
  h2_hier_data[[hier_gb_cols[k]]] <- factor(hier_genres[k], levels = hier_genres)
}
h2_hier_data$sum_within  <- rowSums(h2_hier_data[gh_within])
h2_hier_data$sum_between <- rowSums(h2_hier_data[gh_between])

hier_mm_term <- function(g_cols, x_cols) {
  sprintf("(1 | mm(%s, weights = cbind(%s), scale = FALSE))",
          paste(g_cols, collapse = ", "), paste(x_cols, collapse = ", "))
}
h2_hier_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~ sum_within + sum_between + (1 | pid) +",
  hier_mm_term(hier_gw_cols, gh_within), "+",
  hier_mm_term(hier_gb_cols, gh_between)
))
# brms names an mm group "mm" followed by its member variables.
h2_hier_group_w <- paste0("mm", paste(hier_gw_cols, collapse = ""))
h2_hier_group_b <- paste0("mm", paste(hier_gb_cols, collapse = ""))

# Prior check: every prior is the brms default. The Methods state S = 2.5 for
# every SD (tau_within and tau_between included) and an intercept location
# equal to the rounded sample median (txt_wemwbs_median, chunk txt-priors,
# computed from the same observations); all must match what brms uses.
h2_hier_default_prior <- brms::default_prior(h2_hier_formula, data = h2_hier_data,
                                             family = gaussian())
stopifnot(setequal(unique(h2_hier_default_prior$group[grepl("^mm", h2_hier_default_prior$group)]),
                   c(h2_hier_group_w, h2_hier_group_b)))
sd_default_string <- with(h2_hier_default_prior,
                          prior[class == "sd" & group == "" & coef == ""])
stopifnot(length(sd_default_string) == 1,
          grepl("^student_t\\(3, 0, [0-9.]+\\)$", sd_default_string))
tau_prior_scale <- as.numeric(sub("^student_t\\(3, 0, ([0-9.]+)\\)$", "\\1",
                                  sd_default_string))
intercept_default_string <- with(h2_hier_default_prior, prior[class == "Intercept"])
stopifnot(tau_prior_scale == 2.5,
          txt_wemwbs_median == round(median(h2_hier_data$wemwbs), 1),
          intercept_default_string ==
            sprintf("student_t(3, %s, %s)", round(median(h2_hier_data$wemwbs), 1),
                    tau_prior_scale))

h2_hier_model <- brm(
  formula  = h2_hier_formula,
  data     = h2_hier_data,
  # brms default priors (see above); no prior, no stanvars.
  family   = gaussian(),
  chains   = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000, seed = 2025,
  control  = list(adapt_delta = 0.999, max_treedepth = 15),
  file     = here("models/h2_hier_model_v4")
)

# Draw-wise M3 quantities from a non-centred fit (also used for M3-D in chunk
# daily-fits): gamma = b_sum_*, tau = sd_<mm group>__Intercept, and the
# per-genre coefficients beta_g = gamma + r_<mm group>[g,Intercept]. The mm
# group names are found from the fit's variables (sd_mmgW_... / sd_mmgB_...);
# exactly 14 r_ columns per term must exist, in the order of `genres`.
hier_nc_draws <- function(fit, genres, group_w = NULL, group_b = NULL) {
  vars <- brms::variables(fit)
  find_group <- function(prefix) {
    hit <- vars[grepl(sprintf("^sd_mm%s1%s2.*__Intercept$", prefix, prefix), vars)]
    stopifnot(length(hit) == 1)
    sub("__Intercept$", "", sub("^sd_", "", hit))
  }
  gw <- find_group("gW_")
  gb <- find_group("gB_")
  if (!is.null(group_w)) stopifnot(identical(gw, group_w))
  if (!is.null(group_b)) stopifnot(identical(gb, group_b))
  r_cols <- function(g) {
    cols <- vars[startsWith(vars, paste0("r_", g, "["))]
    lev  <- sub(",Intercept\\]$", "", sub(paste0("r_", g, "["), "", cols, fixed = TRUE))
    stopifnot(length(cols) == 14, identical(lev, genres),
              all(endsWith(cols, ",Intercept]")))
    cols
  }
  rw <- r_cols(gw)
  rb <- r_cols(gb)
  need <- c("b_sum_within", "b_sum_between",
            paste0("sd_", gw, "__Intercept"), paste0("sd_", gb, "__Intercept"), rw, rb)
  stopifnot(all(need %in% vars))
  dr <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit, variable = need)
  gamma_w <- dr$b_sum_within
  gamma_b <- dr$b_sum_between
  beta_w  <- gamma_w + sapply(rw, function(v) dr[[v]])  # draws x 14
  beta_b  <- gamma_b + sapply(rb, function(v) dr[[v]])
  colnames(beta_w) <- colnames(beta_b) <- genres
  list(gamma_w = gamma_w, gamma_b = gamma_b,
       tau_w = dr[[paste0("sd_", gw, "__Intercept")]],
       tau_b = dr[[paste0("sd_", gb, "__Intercept")]],
       beta_w = beta_w, beta_b = beta_b, group_w = gw, group_b = gb)
}
h2_hier_nc <- hier_nc_draws(h2_hier_model, hier_genres,
                            group_w = h2_hier_group_w, group_b = h2_hier_group_b)
