  formula = h2_mm_formula,
  data    = mm_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  # brms default priors (see mm-formula-setup).
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 8000,
  warmup  = 4000,
  seed    = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999, max_treedepth = 15),
  file    = here("models/h2_mm_model_full")
)

Total Playtime (H1)

H1 predicted that total playtime is not meaningfully associated with wellbeing, whether a person plays more or less than usual in a given wave (H1a) or habitually plays more or less than other people (H1b). The preregistered model is M1, the within-between regression of total playtime; we judged each of its two coefficients against the ROPE of ±0.06 points per hour/day. M1 was estimated with Bayesian methods rather than the preregistered frequentist equivalence test (Deviation D3). Under the preregistered decision grid, the preregistered frequentist test reported in Appendix D likewise classified neither coefficient as practically significant. Figure 3 shows the posterior distributions, and Appendix E (Table 10) tabulates all hypothesis tests.

Preregistered Model (M1)

Within persons (H1a), the posterior mean was 0.003 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day (95% CI: [-0.008, 0.014]), with >99.9% of the posterior draws inside the ROPE. In waves in which a participant played more than their own average, wellbeing did not differ by a practically meaningful amount.

Between persons (H1b), the posterior mean was -0.016 (95% CI: [-0.034, 0.002]), with >99.9% of the posterior draws inside the ROPE. The estimate leaned negative, with a credible interval that reached zero, but its magnitude was far below the SESOI: a 2 hour/day difference in habitual playtime corresponded to -0.032 points on the 1–5 scale, about 0.8% of the 4-point range.

Both components of H1 were supported under the ROPE rule (Deviation D3) and under the preregistered 90% CI grid (Appendix D), which classified the within-person coefficient as showing no practically significant association and the between-person coefficient as a negative association that is not practically significant.

M1’s random slope estimates how much the within-person association varies between participants. The SD of the person-specific associations was 0.039 (95% CI: [0.008, 0.065]), and 6.5% of its posterior lay above the SESOI. Under the model’s normal random-slope assumption, this spread combined with the average association implied that the within-person association exceeded the SESOI, in either direction, for about 14.5% of participants. The Discussion returns to this minority.

Exploratory Model (M4)

M4 belongs to H2, but its fixed effects are H1 quantities: the average within-person and between-person associations of total playtime, estimated without assuming that the association is the same for every genre. We report them here beside M1’s; the genre deviations themselves describe the genre differences that H2 concerns and are reported in the next section. M4’s estimates matched M1’s. Within persons, βW = 0.006 (95% CI: [-0.027, 0.042]), with 99.4% of the posterior draws inside the ROPE; between persons, βB = -0.013 (95% CI: [-0.036, 0.011]), with >99.9% of the draws inside (Figure 3). Allowing the association to depend on which genres were played left the total-playtime association unchanged. M2 and M3 have no total-playtime term and do not bear on H1.

Genre Differences (H2)

Our second hypothesis was that genres differ in how playtime relates to wellbeing within persons (H2a) and between persons (H2b). The preregistered model is M2, which estimates a within-person and a between-person coefficient for each of the 14 genres. The exploratory models M3 and M4 estimate the spread of the genre effects as a model parameter. Figure 4 and Figure 5 show these results across the three models.

Preregistered Model (M2)

The preregistered inference for H2 is a joint Wald test of whether the 14 genre coefficients are equal. We fitted a frequentist version of M2 by maximum likelihood, with the same fixed effects and random intercept, and tested the equality of its coefficients. The null hypothesis sets the 13 differences between the first genre’s coefficient and each of the others to zero, which holds only if all 14 coefficients are equal; rejecting it means that at least one difference is non-zero, and hence that at least two genres differ. Within persons, the test rejected equality (χ²(13) = 25.1, p = 0.023): at least two genres differed in how a change in their playtime related to a change in wellbeing. Between persons, the test did not reject equality (χ²(13) = 13.7, p = 0.398). Under the preregistered criteria, H2a was supported and H2b was not. Appendix D reports these tests together with the preregistered H1 equivalence tests, under two preregistered specifications and on the earlier sample that Deviation D7 corrects (Table 5); under the preregistered primary-genre attribution, the within-person test did not reject equality (p = 0.188).

The joint Wald test shows whether the coefficients differ, but not which ones differ or by how much. To describe the size of the differences from the same model, we computed the SD of the 14 genre coefficients at each posterior draw of the Bayesian fit of M2, and from it the descriptors defined in the Methods; none of them was preregistered, and none was converted into a verdict. Within persons, the SD averaged 0.032 (95% CI: [0.02, 0.048]; Figure 4, top row). It implied that 7.2% of genres (95% CI [0.3%, 20.8%]) lay more than 0.06 from the average genre effect, an expected 1.0 of the 14, and that 18.8% of genre pairs (95% CI [3.3%, 37.4%]) differed by more than 0.06. Between persons, the SD averaged 0.078 (95% CI: [0.044, 0.127]), which implied that 42.1% of genres (95% CI [17.7%, 63.8%]) lay more than 0.06 from the average genre effect, an expected 5.9 of the 14, and that 56.5% of genre pairs (95% CI [34%, 73.9%]) differed by more than 0.06. Because M2 estimates the 14 coefficients independently, each carries its own estimation noise, which is large for rarely played genres, and the SD of the 14 estimates, and the shares derived from it, can therefore overstate how much the genres truly differ.

Figure 5 (blue circles) shows the per-genre estimates from M2. The 14 within-person point estimates clustered near zero, and 8 of the 14 credible intervals fell entirely inside the ROPE; the remainder straddled a boundary rather than excluding it. The cost of independent estimation showed in the interval widths: the widest within-person interval (Point-and-Click) was about 5 times wider than the narrowest, too wide to support a conclusion about any rarely played genre. Between persons the intervals were wider still, with 2 of the 14 entirely inside the ROPE.

Exploratory Models (M3 and M4)

M3 and M4 were specified after the M2 results were known. Under M3, the hierarchical prior model, the spread of the within-person genre effects (H2a) was τwithin = 0.016 (95% CI: [0.005, 0.032]; Figure 4, middle row). This spread implied that 0.6% of genres (95% CI [0%, 5.8%]) lay more than 0.06 from the common genre effect, an expected 0.08 of the 14, and that 2.7% of genre pairs (95% CI [0%, 17.9%]) differed by more than 0.06. Between persons (H2b), τbetween = 0.017 (95% CI: [0.001, 0.05]), which implied that 2.5% of genres (95% CI [0%, 22.6%]) lay more than 0.06 from the common genre effect, an expected 0.35 of the 14, and that 6.2% of genre pairs (95% CI [0%, 39.2%]) differed by more than 0.06. The prior on τ places 0.9% of its mass below the reference value of 0.031, against 97.1% of the posterior for τwithin, so the concentration of τwithin at small values came from the data rather than the prior. M3 estimated the common genre effects at γW = 0.002 within persons (95% CI: [-0.009, 0.015]) and γB = -0.007 between persons (95% CI: [-0.022, 0.010]); the means of the 14 independently estimated M2 coefficients were 0.007 (95% CI: [-0.003, 0.017]) and -0.010 (95% CI: [-0.037, 0.017]), respectively.

Under M4, the multi-membership model, the spread of the within-person genre adjustments (H2a) was \sigma_{s,\text{within}} = 0.045 (95% CI: [0.006, 0.101]; Figure 4, bottom row). This spread implied that 18.4% of genres (95% CI [0%, 55.3%]) deviated from the overall playtime slope by more than 0.06, an expected 2.6 of the 14, and that 30.4% of genre pairs (95% CI [0%, 67.5%]) differed by more than 0.06; spreads up to the upper credible bound of 0.101 points per hour/day remained plausible. Between persons (H2b), \sigma_{s,\text{between}} = 0.017 (95% CI: [0.001, 0.045]), which implied that 2% of genres (95% CI [0%, 18.3%]) deviated from the overall playtime slope by more than 0.06, an expected 0.28 of the 14, and that 5.6% of genre pairs (95% CI [0%, 34.7%]) differed by more than 0.06.

The three estimates in Figure 4 measure the spread of the genre effects in different ways. M2 estimates each genre independently, so its 14 coefficients are noisy and the SD across them can overstate the spread. M3 and M4 instead pool information across genres: a hierarchical model shrinks the noisier estimates towards the common centre, which reduces the impact of noise and of multiple comparisons (Gelman et al., 2012). Within persons, M4’s σs was less precise than M3’s τ, because it describes how the playtime slope changes with the genre composition of a wave rather than how separate genre exposures differ.

M3 shrinks the per-genre estimates towards the common genre effect (Figure 5, orange squares): 14 of the 14 within-person credible intervals fell entirely inside the ROPE, as did 12 of the 14 wider between-person intervals.

M4 estimates each genre as a deviation from the overall playtime slope (Figure 5, purple diamonds). With the overall fixed effect added back, its within-person estimates spanned -0.024 to 0.048 and its between-person estimates -0.032 to -0.005.

The spread describes how far the genre effects lie from one another. Whether the associations are practically null in every genre depends on where the genre effects are centred as well as on their spread, so we also computed, at each posterior draw, the share of each model’s genre-effect distribution lying outside the ROPE (Vuorre, Kay, et al., 2024). Within persons, that share was 8.1% under M2 (95% CI: [0.3%, 22.9%]), 0.8% under M3 (95% CI: [0%, 7.3%]), and 20.5% under M4 (95% CI: [0%, 57.7%]); between persons, it was 43.1% under M2 (95% CI: [19.1%, 64.8%]), 3% under M3 (95% CI: [0%, 25.1%]), and 3.3% under M4 (95% CI: [0%, 24.3%]). Within persons, the share was smallest under M3; the M2 shares were inflated by the wide intervals of rarely played genres, and the M4 shares reflected uncertainty in both the spread and the overall playtime slope.

In sum, the preregistered tests answered H2: the within-person genre coefficients were not all equal, so H2a was supported (although not under the preregistered primary-genre attribution; Appendix D), and the between-person test did not detect differences, so H2b was not. The spreads described how large the within-person differences were. Under M3, an expected 0.08 of the 14 genres lay more than 0.06 from the common genre effect and 2.7% of genre pairs differed by more than 0.06; the corresponding figures were 1.0 genres and 18.8% of pairs under M2, whose SD includes estimation noise, and 2.6 genres and 30.4% of pairs under M4, whose spread was less precisely estimated. As set out in the Methods, we do not convert these quantities into a verdict on the practical size of the genre differences. Between persons, M2’s SD was inflated by the noise in the wide between-person intervals: its upper credible bound was more than twice that of M3’s τbetween. Genre terms did not improve out-of-sample prediction (Appendix D), and the wide intervals for rarely played genres ruled out confident inference about any single genre. Appendix E (Table 10) tabulates the joint tests, the spread estimates and their descriptors, and the convergence diagnostics for the three models; full posterior summaries for all four models are in the supplementary materials.

Daily Timescale (Exploratory)

The daily-level analyses (M1-D to M4-D) were not preregistered, and every estimate in this section is exploratory. Participants in the analysed daily sample contributed a median of 21 diary days, with participation declining from 888 responses on day 1 to 384 on day 30; windows closed at the survey completion timestamp (median length 13.7 hours), so 60.6% of person-days recorded no console or PC play.

Figure 6 displays the posteriors against the ROPE. At the daily level, the within-person association between same-day playtime and life satisfaction was positive, at β = 0.18 points per additional hour in the standalone total-playtime model (M1-D; 95% CI [0.01, 0.35]), with the lower credible bound at zero and >99.9% of the posterior draws inside the ROPE; the multi-membership model’s fixed effect was similar (M4-D: β = 0.14, 95% CI [-0.27, 0.49]). The interval widened past zero under two of the three robustness refits (Appendix D). Person-to-person variation in this slope was practically negligible: the random-slope SD was 0.73 (95% CI [0.4, 1.02]), with 96.5% of the posterior below the SESOI. Between persons, with habitual play measured in full-day hours, participants who played more than others reported slightly lower daily life satisfaction: M1-D gave β = -0.38 points per habitual daily hour (95% CI [-1.11, 0.34]), a negative lean whose posterior sat 95.3% inside the ROPE; M4-D gave β = -0.41 (95% CI [-1.17, 0.34]); and the all-responses refit, which scores unobserved play as zero, gave β = -0.37 (95% CI [-1.11, 0.3]) (Table 11).

At the daily level, we described the genre spreads with the same quantities as at the biweekly level, with the daily SESOI of one slider point per hour in place of 0.06, and again without a verdict; the corresponding reference values are 0.51 slider points (1 ÷ 1.96) for genre effects around their average and 0.36 (1 ÷ (1.96 × √2)) for genre pairs. Within persons, the hierarchical prior gave τwithin = 0.22 (95% CI [0.01, 0.57]), which implied an expected 0.10 of the 14 genres more than one point from the common genre effect and 2.7% of genre pairs more than one point apart. The multi-membership model gave σs,within = 0.44 (95% CI [0.02, 1.21]; an expected 1.00 genres and 14.1% of pairs), and the per-draw SD of M2-D’s 14 independently estimated coefficients, inflated by estimation error as at the biweekly level, was 0.63 (95% CI [0.41, 0.87]; an expected 1.6 genres and 25.8% of pairs). Between persons, τbetween = 0.9 (95% CI [0.06, 2.15]; an expected 3.5 genres and 36.6% of pairs), σs,between = 0.2 (95% CI [0.01, 0.71]; an expected 0.17 genres and 3.1% of pairs), and M2-D’s between-person raw SD was 2.4 (95% CI [1.5, 3.53]; an expected 9.3 genres and 75.8% of pairs), again inflated by estimation error.

Robustness

Two sensitivity analyses tested whether the conclusions depended on analytic choices. Neither changed the H1 conclusion. Adjusting for age, gender, and ethnicity shifted the H1 coefficients by less than 0.01 points and changed no ROPE verdict (Appendix D, Table 6). Refitting on multiply imputed data (m = 100) left neither H1 coefficient practically significant under the preregistered 90% CI grid (equivalence tests are two one-sided tests at α = .05, which correspond to a 90% rather than a 95% interval; Lakens (2017)) but, unlike the complete-case analysis, rejected genre-coefficient equality in neither pooled dimension (Appendix D, Table 8). Appendix D gives full specifications, results, and diagnostics for both analyses, together with the predictive model comparison and the preregistered frequentist analyses (Table 5): no H1 coefficient was practically significant under the preregistered grid with mobile play included or on the earlier sample, and the within-person joint test for H2 rejected equality under full but not under primary genre attribution.

Discussion

When previous work has reported that time spent gaming carries no meaningful association with wellbeing, a common objection is that surely it must depend on the type of game one plays. After all, a relaxing puzzle game and a competitive shooter should not plausibly have the same effect on the person playing them. Video game heterogeneity is the standing explanation for why aggregate playtime nulls should not be taken at face value: playtime is a poorly specified exposure whose associations average over distinct causal contrasts (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025; Magnusson et al., 2024), and a null total association can in principle be produced by heterogeneous true effects that offset in aggregate (Yarkoni, 2022). Genre is the most widely used name for those contrasts (Starosta et al., 2024), which makes it the natural first place to look.

Continued debate about how different games might differ in their effects on wellbeing persists in part because of measurement challenges, whereby prior genre research has been subject to at least one of three limitations, and usually multiple. First, genre assignment is inconsistent and unreliable: labels are typically self-assigned by participants or researchers, the same games are classified into different genres across studies, and nearly all taxonomies force each game into a single genre despite modern games being multi-genre by design (King et al., 2019; Starosta et al., 2024). Second, playtime has often been self-reported rather than logged, yet self-reported and logged media use correlate only moderately, with a meta-analytic estimate of r = 0.38 and fewer than one in ten self-reports falling within 5% of the logged value (Parry et al., 2021). Our own positive control, which compared self-reported biweekly playtime with the logged total, gave r = 0.483: somewhat above the meta-analytic value, but still a correlation at which self-reports share only 23% of their variance with logged play, and one that may be depressed because the self-reports can also cover play on platforms outside our telemetry. Self-report and telemetry therefore agree on who plays more and who plays less, but too loosely to stand in for one another. Third, studies often cover a single game or a handful of titles (Brühlmann et al., 2020; Johannes et al., 2021; Larrieu et al., 2023), leaving genre contrasts to be assembled across different studies that classified and measured both play and genre incommensurably, and often years apart in a medium whose genre labels drift as it evolves (Cohen, 1986; Vargas-Iglesias, 2020), so that a label such as adventure need not have covered the same games in each.

This study represents an advancement on all three fronts. Genre labels follow a single crowd-sourced taxonomy applied uniformly to every title across all platforms, retaining multiple genre labels where relevant. Playtime is measured as objective session-level telemetry across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam rather than self-reported. And all 14 genres are estimated jointly within a single sample, so genre contrasts emerge from one dataset with a common measurement of play, genre, and wellbeing.

The playtime-wellbeing association is practically equivalent to zero

When participants played more than their own average in a given two-week wave, their wellbeing barely changed, consistent with previous digital trace studies that have repeatedly found aggregate playtime to be a poor predictor of wellbeing fluctuations (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Larrieu et al., 2023). Between participants, practical equivalence was likewise established.

Inverting the estimates shows what these associations would amount to even if they were causal. Within persons, wellbeing would shift by one minimally important difference only after roughly 101 additional hours of play per day at the point estimate, and after 21 additional hours at the credible bound most favourable to an association, more extreme than the 10 additional daily hours that Vuorre et al. (2022) derived from game-level telemetry. Between participants, the habitual difference needed to reach the same threshold lies between 9 and 19 hours of daily play. Both requirements exceed the roughly five hours of leisure that US adults have in a day (Sturm & Cohen, 2019), and changes of this order do not occur in practice: of the 1,434 participants observed across adjacent waves, only 116 ever changed their average daily play by 4 or more hours from one wave to the next. An association that no achievable play exposure can reach is, for every practical purpose, indistinguishable from no association at all.

The contrast between light and heavy players deserves one further remark. Participants who habitually play more reported slightly lower average wellbeing, yet the same participants’ wellbeing did not fall in waves when they played more than usual. This within-null, between-negative pattern recurs across observational media research and is most plausibly a selection effect, in which people with lower baseline wellbeing spend more time in games rather than games lowering wellbeing (Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Kievit et al., 2013; Robinson, 1950; Rohrer & Murayama, 2023), although a cumulative effect accruing over years would look the same at these timescales (cf. Vuorre et al., 2022). Whichever explanation holds, the difference is too small to matter, so public claims about gamers’ mental health are, in effect, reports about who plays, not about what playing does.

The causal estimates from Japanese console lotteries point the other way, at 0.2 to 0.5 standard deviations per additional daily hour among lottery winners who acquired a console because they won (Egami et al., 2024; Egami et al., 2026). Those are local effects of acquiring a new console, measured with self-reported play over the preceding month and diminishing at longer play durations, whereas our within-person estimates describe logged deviations from each person’s usual playtime among people who already play. The two estimands need not agree: gaining access to a console and playing an extra hour on a console one already owns are different versions of the same nominal exposure (Magnusson et al., 2024).

Associations are close to zero in every genre

We expected genres to differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing. The preregistered joint test supports this prediction within persons, where the 14 genre coefficients are not all equal, but not between persons, and under the preregistered primary-genre attribution neither test rejects equality (Appendix D). The differences it detects lie between genre effects that are all close to zero: under the hierarchical prior, the 14 within-person genre estimates span only -0.020 to +0.016, with no estimate more than a third of the SESOI from zero, and the most-played genres by total playtime (Role-playing, Adventure, Strategy, Shooter; see Figure 2) sit inside this same narrow band. The spread estimated by the same model implies an expected 0.08 of the 14 genres more than 0.06 from the average genre effect and 2.7% of genre pairs more than 0.06 apart, and on average 0.8% of its within-person and 3% of its between-person genre-effect distribution lie outside the ROPE. The multi-membership model is less precise than the hierarchical prior model: its fitted spread implies that about 18% of genres (95% CI [0%, 55%]) deviate from the average slope by more than 0.06, an expected 7.7 of the 14 genres at the upper credible bound, so differences confined to a few genres cannot be excluded. Inference about single genres is limited as well, because the credible intervals for rarely played genres remain wide: under the preregistered model, the widest within-person interval (Point-and-Click) is about 5 times wider than the narrowest. Genres were statistically distinguishable only within persons and only when each game counted towards all its genres, and under the hierarchical prior no genre’s estimated association approached the SESOI; any defence of playtime nulls that appeals to the heterogeneous nature of video games must look to partitions finer than genre.

This result does not contradict the genre differences reported before, because those concern other outcomes and other designs. The most consistent findings involve gaming disorder symptoms, where MMORPG, shooter, and strategy play stand out in cross-sectional surveys of self-reported genre preference (Elliott et al., 2012; King et al., 2019; Na et al., 2017; Rehbein et al., 2021), and player experience, where genres differ in immersion, autonomy, and frustration (Hazel et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2015). Genre also explains little of why people play: among more than 14,000 highly engaged players, correlations between six gaming motives and genre preference ranged from −0.25 to 0.20 (Király et al., 2022). Our estimand, the association between logged exposure to a genre and general wellbeing, is different, and on that estimand every genre’s association lies close to zero.

A Susceptible Minority Is Possible but Small

Still, a null average could conceal a minority for whom play, in total or in specific genres, genuinely matters (cf. Karhulahti et al., 2025). The random slope in M1 addresses the total-playtime case by modelling each participant’s own within-person association between playtime and wellbeing. The relevant quantity is the share of participants the model implies lie beyond the SESOI: combining the posterior for the average within-person effect with the posterior for the person-level slope standard deviation (0.039, 95% CI [0.008, 0.065]) under the model’s normality assumption, an estimated 14.5% of participants (95% CI [0%, 36%]) have a true within-person association exceeding 0.06 SWEMWBS points per daily hour in either direction. A susceptible minority is therefore entirely compatible with our results; what the data constrain is that such susceptibility is neither common nor, for most of the distribution, large at these timescales. Person-specific slope estimates are heavily shrunk towards the mean given the number of waves per participant, so the model quantifies how heavy the tails are without being able to identify which individuals occupy them; targeted designs with denser within-person sampling would be needed for that.

Shortening the Window Does Not Recover an Effect

A further possibility is temporal, namely that the wellbeing effects of play might surface and dissipate faster than a biweekly retrospective survey can register. To test this claim, the exploratory daily analysis shortens the window from fourteen days to one and reproduces the total-playtime conclusion. Within persons, every total-playtime estimate lies inside the equivalence region under every specification, and the same-day point estimate is positive, roughly double its biweekly counterpart in within-person standard-deviation units (0.015 versus 0.008 sw per hour). The direction is consistent with the session-level affective uplift reported among PowerWash Simulator players (Vuorre, Ballou, et al., 2024), though its resolution is fragile across the robustness refits and should be read as suggestive. Its practical magnitude is negligible either way: shifting daily life satisfaction by one minimally important difference (5 points on the 0–100 slider, the daily counterpart of the 0.3-point SWEMWBS difference behind the preregistered SESOI) would require 28 additional hours of same-day play, and under the hierarchical prior the daily within-person genre spread implies an expected 0.10 of the 14 genres more than one slider point per hour from the common genre effect. Therefore, moving the measurement closer in time, on its own, does not conjure a meaningful effect.

Are all games the same?

The question this study set out to answer rests on an undisputed fact, that games differ psychologically, and although current genre labels are not an effective way to operationalise those differences when it comes to wellbeing outcomes, the general intuition persists. Game scholars have argued for decades that genre labels are conventions of marketing and library organisation rather than coherent descriptions of play: they conflate gameplay style, purpose, and mood in a single word (Lee et al., 2014), fail elementary classificatory tests (Clarke et al., 2017), and drift as the medium evolves (Cohen, 1986; Vargas-Iglesias, 2020). Even the literature most committed to genre-specific effects has reached the same conclusion: the researchers who documented attentional benefits of action games now argue that industry genre labels have become poor proxies for the mechanics that produce those benefits, and call for a taxonomy of the processes engaged during play instead (Bavelier & Green, 2019; Nguyen & Bavelier, 2023). Games within one genre can differ sharply in structure, as Call of Duty and Halo do within the shooter genre (Saini & Hodgins, 2023). The pathways plausibly connecting play to wellbeing seem to operate at levels that genre labels cannot index (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025). For example, need satisfaction depends on autonomy-supportive design features (Ballou et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2012), social capital depends on co-play relationships (Depping et al., 2018; Vella et al., 2015), and affect regulation depends on the match between gameplay and current emotional state (Kosa et al., 2020).

The broader point is that, as many have argued theoretically but have lacked empirical data to show conclusively, other aspects of game play besides genre are likely more meaningful for wellbeing. Structural characteristics (e.g., avatar customisability) are one such aspect, and dedicated taxonomies now exist for characterising these (e.g., Saini & Hodgins, 2023). In-game behaviour is another: within a single game, behavioural variation in how people play is linked to meaningful wellbeing differences even when genre is held constant (e.g., Hakman et al., 2026). How players fit gaming into their lives is a third: among casual Nintendo players, self-rated gaming life fit predicted wellbeing an order of magnitude more strongly than any playtime measure (Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025). Community-assigned tags that describe mechanics, themes, and social structure may offer a practical middle ground between genre labels and title-level coding (Li, 2020; Starosta et al., 2024).

Our data leave two parts of this picture untested. Mobile games were recorded only as daily minutes without titles; they enter only the first positive control and the preregistered all-platform H1 test in Appendix D, which likewise finds no practically significant association, and none of the genre analyses (see Limitations). Monetisation is the other: free-to-play models, loot boxes, and the related design features that have been argued to harm players (Rehbein et al., 2021; Saini & Hodgins, 2023) need not be spread evenly across genres, so a genre contrast may partly carry a monetisation contrast; in one clinical sample the two were entangled closely enough that the authors proposed monetisation model as the more tractable partition (André et al., 2024).

Methodological Contribution: A Model for Overlapping Categories

Methodologically, the multi-membership model transfers beyond games. To our knowledge this is the first application in media psychology of the model class, developed originally for educational data where students attend multiple schools (Cafri et al., 2015; Fielding & Goldstein, 2006). Any media effects question with overlapping content labels has the same structure (e.g., streaming titles with multiple genre tags, news diets spanning outlets with overlapping orientations, social media feeds spanning topic categories) and can be answered with the same model. Our code is freely available to support future applications of this method.

Limitations

Several limitations constrain these conclusions and point at the work that should come next. First, the design is observational. The within-person decomposition removes stable confounds but not time-varying ones, and players themselves name illness, grief, work pressure, and caretaking as events that move both play and wellbeing, sometimes in opposite directions (Ballou, Földes, Hakman, et al., 2025); our causal statements are correspondingly guarded (Rohrer & Murayama, 2023). Second, the SWEMWBS is a global instrument assessed over a two-week recall window. Gaming sits alongside factors like sleep, work, and social life for wellbeing variance, and domain-specific outcomes (affect, sleep, connectedness) could show associations a global measure averages away. The exploratory daily analysis takes one step down this temporal hierarchy, but future work should consider pairing session-level telemetry with momentary assessments and using time-use data to partial gaming from competing activities. Third, coverage is imperfect: some participants used additional platforms whose telemetry we could not capture, Nintendo telemetry covers first-party titles only (Ballou, Földes, Vuorre, et al., 2025), the main and genre analyses excluded mobile play, which was recorded only as daily minutes without titles or metadata and enters only the first positive control and the preregistered all-platform H1 test in Appendix D, and in-study minutes are dominated by Steam (84.3%, versus 12.9% Xbox and 2.8% Nintendo), so the genre findings are predominantly findings about PC play by UK and US adults. Fourth, participants were adults aged 18 to 40 at screening, so our conclusions say nothing about children or adolescents, for whom both play patterns and susceptibility may differ. Nor do they extend to disordered play in clinical or at-risk populations, where genre-linked structural characteristics remain plausibly relevant (André et al., 2024; Rehbein et al., 2021). Stated as constraints on generality (Simons et al., 2017), our conclusions apply to adults aged 18 to 40 in the UK and US, to console and PC play recorded during the Open Play study period, and to the IGDB genre taxonomy; we have no reason to believe they depend on other characteristics of the sample, but they have not been tested beyond it.

Appendix A: Deviations from Preregistration

This appendix lists all deviations from the Stage 1 preregistration (Ballou, Földes, et al., 2024) in the structured disclosure format of Willroth and Atherton (2024): the original wording, what was done instead, the reason, the timing relative to data access and results, and the impact on interpretation. Analyses that were not preregistered (M3, M4, and the daily-timescale analysis) are not deviations and are labelled exploratory where they appear. Changes made upstream during data collection, outside the authors’ control, are consolidated as D6. D7 records a restriction of the analytic sample that followed a correction in a later upstream data release.

# Topic Type Timing
D1 Genre assignment by full attribution Data preparation After data access, before results known
D2 Genre taxonomy Data preparation After data access, before results known
D3 Bayesian estimation and priors Inferential criteria After data access, before results known
D4 H1 platform scope without mobile Variables After data access, before results known
D5 Missing-data protocol Analytic approach After complete-case results known
D6 Upstream data-collection changes Data collection procedures During data collection, before data access
D7 Analytic sample restricted to qualified participants Data exclusions After data access and after results known

Structured disclosures

D1: Genre assignment by full attribution

Field Content
Type Data preparation
Original wording Games are classified by their primary (first) IGDB genre.
Deviation description A game’s full playtime counts towards every one of its IGDB genre labels (up to 16 per game). Genre hours are therefore exposures to games carrying each label and are not mutually exclusive; total playtime for H1 is computed separately from raw sessions.
Reason Most games carry several labels; using only the first discards classification information and depends on IGDB’s label order.
Timing After data access, before results known
Reader impact Each genre coefficient estimates the association with exposure to games carrying that label, not the effect of a genre in isolation. Under the preregistered primary-genre attribution, the within-person joint Wald test does not reject the equality of the genre coefficients (p = 0.188), whereas it does under full attribution (p = 0.023), so the support for H2a depends on this choice (Appendix D, Table 5, primary-attribution rows).

D2: Genre taxonomy

Field Content
Type Data preparation
Original wording IGDB sub-genres are collapsed as follows: Hack and slash/Beat ’em up → Action; Point-and-click and Visual Novel → Adventure; Turn-based strategy, Real-time strategy, and Tactical → Strategy; Quiz/Trivia → Puzzle.
Deviation description Hack-and-slash/Beat-’em-up, Point-and-click, and Visual Novel are kept as separate categories; MOBA joins Strategy, Card & Board Game joins Puzzle, Pinball and Music join Arcade, and Indie is dropped as a non-substantive label, giving 14 categories (Appendix B).
Reason The preregistered collapsing merged genres that prior literature treats as psychologically distinct.
Timing After data access, before results known
Reader impact Per-genre estimates refer to different category boundaries than the preregistration implies. The retained sub-genres are rarely played and have wide credible intervals.

D3: Bayesian estimation and priors

Field Content
Type Inferential criteria
Original wording H1: equivalence test (TOST) with SESOI = ±0.06 SWEMWBS points per hour/day, using 90% CIs. H2: joint Wald test via car::linearHypothesis(). No priors are specified (all models frequentist).
Deviation description M1 and M2 are estimated as Bayesian multilevel models with brms (Bürkner, 2017) rather than with lmer. H1 is evaluated against the preregistered ROPE [−0.06, +0.06], with a 95% credible interval entirely inside the ROPE establishing practical equivalence (Kruschke, 2018), in place of the preregistered decision grid for the 90% confidence interval (Methods; Appendix D). The preregistered joint Wald test for H2 is retained on the frequentist counterpart of M2 and answers H2; the size of any departure is described, without a verdict, by the posterior SD of M2’s genre coefficients and the shares of genres and genre pairs it implies beyond the SESOI (Methods). All priors are the brms defaults: improper flat priors on the coefficients, a Student-t(3, 3.3, 2.5) prior on the intercept, centred at the sample median of SWEMWBS, and half-Student-t(3, 0, 2.5) priors on the standard deviations (Appendix F). An earlier version used weakly informative priors; the switch to the defaults was made after those results were known.
Reason Alongside the decision, the ROPE gives a continuous measure of practical equivalence (the posterior share inside it). With flat priors on the slopes, the data alone determine their estimates, so the Bayesian estimates are directly comparable with the preregistered maximum-likelihood analysis.
Timing After data access, before results known (Bayesian estimation); the switch to the brms default priors was made after the results of the earlier priors were known
Reader impact The SESOI and the equivalence region are unchanged, so the risk of bias is low. All priors are the brms defaults (Appendix F), so no analyst-chosen prior scale enters the models. The preregistered frequentist analyses, with the equivalence tests on 90% confidence intervals and the joint Wald tests, are reported in full in Appendix D (Preregistered Frequentist Analysis, Table 5).

D4: H1 platform scope without mobile

Field Content
Type Variables
Original wording H1 uses total playtime across all five platforms (Nintendo, Xbox, Steam, iOS, Android).
Deviation description H1 total playtime uses Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam only. Mobile platforms provide daily minutes without game titles (D6), so including them for H1 but not for H2 would give “total playtime” two different meanings.
Reason Consistency between H1 and H2.
Timing After data access, before results known
Reader impact Mobile play is omitted from the H1 exposure; it made up 3.3% of all-platform playtime in the analysed person-waves, and the preregistered all-platform H1 model likewise finds no practically significant association in either dimension (Appendix D, Table 5, all-platform rows). The findings do not speak to mobile play.

D5: Missing-data protocol

Field Content
Type Analytic approach
Original wording Multiple imputation via mice (predictive mean matching, wide format); report both complete-case and imputed results.
Deviation description Wave nonresponse rather than item missingness dominates: 3,355 of 9,648 person-waves (34.8%) have no SWEMWBS. We therefore imputed on the full participant × wave grid with two-level MICE (2l.pmm, participants as clusters; m = 100 by von Hippel’s rule) and report pooled frequentist results alongside the complete-case Bayesian models (Appendix D).
Reason Single-level wide-format PMM ignores the hierarchical structure and cannot address wave nonresponse.
Timing Adopted after the complete-case results were known; the protocol was taken over unchanged from the sibling Stage 2 studies of the same programmatic report rather than tailored to these results
Reader impact The H1 conclusions are unchanged under imputation, whereas the pooled within-person joint test for H2 does not reject the equality of the genre coefficients, unlike the complete-case test; the pooled between-person H1 interval widens because person means are uncertain for participants with few observed waves. Agreement between complete-case and imputed H1 results does not rule out bias from nonresponse that depends on unobserved wellbeing.

D6: Upstream data-collection changes

Field Content
Type Data collection procedures
Original wording Age range 18–75 (UK) and 18–30 (US); at least 75% of gaming time on included platforms; Android telemetry as session-level ActivityWatch exports.
Deviation description Made by the Open Play team before this study’s data access: screening admitted ages 18–40 in both regions, the coverage threshold was lowered to 50%, and Android data were collected as daily minutes from Digital Wellbeing screenshots. Reported in full by Ballou, Földes, Vuorre, et al. (2025).
Reason Recruitment and data-collection constraints upstream; outside the authors’ control.
Timing During data collection, before data access
Reader impact Findings generalise to adults aged 18–40; the lower coverage threshold adds measurement error to total playtime; Android contributes daily totals only (see D4).

D7: Analytic sample restricted to qualified participants

Field Content
Type Data exclusions
Original wording Those who “(1) self-report playing video games, (2) self-report that at least 75% of their total video game play takes place on the platforms included in the study, and (3) are willing to link all relevant gaming accounts will be invited to complete an intake survey”; participants without playtime logged on any self-reported platform during a 7-day baseline are excluded before the panel surveys. “We do not preregister any further exclusion criteria.”
Deviation description The analytic sample is restricted to participants whose intake record is flagged as qualified in Open Play v1.2.6. Release v1.2.4 revoked this flag for 306 intakes of participants who had entered the surveys without passing the account-linking and telemetry validation; 133 of them had been in our earlier analytic sample and are now excluded. The same rule excludes 97 participants of the earlier sample whose biweekly responses carry a participant identifier that matches no intake record in any release. We traced this to the data provider’s survey export, which takes the identifier from each survey response without checking it against the intake table, so that responses whose identifier differs from the one on the exported intake record, or whose intake was never completed, appear as participants without a screening record; we reported it to the Open Play team. Their qualification cannot be established from the release, and the cleaned release files hold no console or PC telemetry for them. The analytic sample is 1,608 participants.
Reason An upstream correction of the eligibility flag, described in the release notes as false positives. Most participants whose flag was revoked had not met the preregistered linking and telemetry criteria: of the 133 in the earlier sample, 63 had never linked an account and 65 have no console or PC telemetry at all, so their zero playtime was unobserved rather than recorded. The participants without an intake record have no screening record under that identifier and no console or PC telemetry in the cleaned release files, so their exposure is unknown. Retaining either group would have entered missing exposure as zero play.
Timing After data access and after the results were known; triggered by the August 2026 data release, not by the results
Reader impact The sample is smaller, and estimates refer to participants whose playtime was validly observed. In frequentist refits of the preregistered models on the earlier sample (1,838 participants) and on the corrected sample, the within-person slope is practically unchanged (0.0028 and 0.0028), the between-person slope moves slightly towards zero (from -0.0167 [-0.0313, -0.0022] to -0.0157 [-0.0309, -0.0004], 90% CIs), the preregistered decision grid gives the same H1 verdicts on both samples (no practically significant association within persons; a negative association that is not practically significant between persons), and both joint Wald tests reach the same decisions (within: p = 0.024 and 0.023; between: p = 0.385 and 0.398; Appendix D, Table 5).

Appendix B: Genre Mapping

Genre labels from all three platforms resolve to the study taxonomy in two steps: Xbox store labels are first mapped onto IGDB genres (per the preregistration’s Appendix B), and raw IGDB labels (23 distinct labels observed in the study metadata) are then collapsed into 14 analysis-level categories. Table 2 presents both steps in one place: each row is an implemented study genre, with the raw IGDB labels it subsumes, the Xbox store labels routed to it, and, where the preregistered mapping (which would yield 17 distinct genres on the observed labels) treated a label differently, the preregistered assignment. The implemented mapping diverges from the preregistered one in both directions: it preserves granularity for sub-genres that prior literature treats as distinct (Hack-and-slash/Beat-’em-up, Point-and-click, Visual Novel), collapses more aggressively elsewhere (MOBA into Strategy, Card & Board Game into Puzzle, Pinball and Music into Arcade), and excludes Indie as a non-substantive label (see Appendix A, Deviation D2). Two details sit outside the table: the Xbox label Family + Kids has no IGDB equivalent and is resolved by the title’s secondary genre, and IGDB includes no top-level “Action” category, so what is colloquially called “action” is distributed across Shooter, Hack-and-slash, Fighting, and Platform.

Appendix D: Sensitivity and Supplementary Analyses

This appendix first reports the preregistered frequentist analyses, on the analytic sample, under two preregistered specifications, and on the earlier sample that Deviation D7 corrects. It then reports the two sensitivity analyses summarised under Robustness in the main text: demographic covariate adjustment and multiple imputation of wave nonresponse (with distributional diagnostics). The predictive model comparison (whether genre terms improve out-of-sample prediction) follows, and finally the design details and sensitivity refits of the daily-timescale analysis.

Preregistered Frequentist Analysis

The preregistered analyses were frequentist: H1 was to be tested by an equivalence test on the 90% confidence intervals of the within-between model of total playtime, and H2 by joint Wald tests of the equality of the genre coefficients, both on multilevel models fitted with lme4. The Bayesian models in the main text are the models we interpret (Deviation D3), and the Results report the preregistered H2 tests on the analytic sample. This subsection reports all preregistered tests in one place (Table 5): on the analytic sample, under the two preregistered specifications from which the main analysis departs, total playtime across all five platforms for H1 (Deviation D4) and primary-genre attribution for H2 (Deviation D1), and on the earlier analytic sample that Deviation D7 corrects. The all-platform total adds each wave’s iOS and Android gaming minutes to its Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam playtime; 164 participants had mobile minutes in at least one analysed person-wave, and 9.2% of the analysed person-waves had any. Under primary attribution, each game’s full playtime counts towards its first IGDB genre label that remains in the 14-genre taxonomy (Appendix B), so genre exposures are mutually exclusive. The earlier sample comprises the 1,838 participants with at least one valid SWEMWBS in Open Play v1.2.1, without the qualification condition, and its analysis frame was built from the v1.2.1 files with the same code as the main frame. Each H1 model has a random intercept and a correlated random slope for within-person playtime, as preregistered, and was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood; each H2 model was fitted by maximum likelihood with a random intercept, because the preregistered uncorrelated random slopes gave a singular fit in all three H2 analyses (table note). H1 verdicts follow the preregistered decision grid of the Stage 1 Design Table, applied to the lower (LB) and upper (UB) bounds of the 90% confidence interval: LB > 0.06 or UB < −0.06 indicates a practically significant positive or negative association; LB > 0 and UB > 0.06, or UB < 0 and LB < −0.06, a positive or negative association that may be practically significant; LB > 0 and UB < 0.06, or UB < 0 and LB > −0.06, a positive or negative association that is not practically significant; LB > −0.06 and UB < 0.06 with an interval that covers zero, no practically significant association; and an interval that covers zero and one or both bounds, an inconclusive result. The Design Table lists the absence of a practically significant association for every interval inside ±0.06, including those that exclude zero, and we applied the more specific classes to the latter; it also gives the first bound as LB > −0.06, which we read as LB > 0.06, the counterpart of UB < −0.06. H2 is supported if the joint test rejects equality at α = .05.

Under the preregistered grid, the within-person coefficient on the analytic sample, 0.0028 [-0.0067, 0.0122], showed no practically significant association, and the between-person coefficient, -0.0157 [-0.0309, -0.0004], a negative association that is not practically significant: its interval excluded zero but lay inside ±0.06. The earlier sample gave the same two verdicts. Mobile play made up 3.3% of all-platform playtime in the analysed person-waves. With it included, the within-person verdict was unchanged, and the between-person interval, -0.0150 [-0.0302, 0.0002], included zero, so this coefficient showed no practically significant association. None of the 6 H1 rows showed an association that is, or may be, practically significant. On the analytic sample under full attribution, the within-person joint test rejected the equality of the genre coefficients (p = 0.023) and the between-person test did not (p = 0.398), so H2a was supported and H2b was not; the earlier sample gave the same decisions (p = 0.024 and p = 0.385). Under the preregistered primary-genre attribution, neither test rejected equality (within: χ²(13) = 17.2, p = 0.188; between: χ²(13) = 14.8, p = 0.321), so the support for H2a depended on the attribution rule. Primary attribution assigns each multi-genre game to a single genre, which leaves genres that are seldom listed first with few players: Visual Novel was the primary genre of games played by 6 participants, whereas 129 participants played games carrying the label. Its between-person coefficient had a standard error of 5.07, and the SD of the other 13 between-person coefficients was 0.121, so the between-person SD of 0.957 under primary attribution reflected the estimation error of this genre rather than a spread across genres.

Demographic Covariates

The preregistration specified a sensitivity analysis adjusting the primary models for demographic covariates. We refit M1 (total playtime) and M2 (independent genre coefficients) with age, gender, and ethnicity added as population-level predictors, using the subset of participants with complete demographic data.

The adjusted models used 6,241 observations from 1,565 participants with complete demographic data. Table 6 compares the primary and covariate-adjusted estimates. The H1 coefficients shifted by at most 0.005 points after adjustment, and the ROPE conclusions were unchanged: >99.9% of the adjusted within-person posterior draws fell inside the ROPE (primary: >99.9%), and >99.9% of the adjusted between-person posterior draws (primary: >99.9%). One qualification: the adjusted between-person credible interval ([-0.04, -0.002]) excluded zero, unlike the unadjusted interval; this small negative association remained far inside the ROPE and is consistent with the selection account discussed under H1. The genre heterogeneity estimates were likewise essentially unaffected. Both adjusted models converged cleanly (max R-hat = 1.005, 0 divergent transitions). Demographic composition therefore did not account for the observed associations.

Multiple Imputation

The preregistration specified multiple imputation by chained equations with predictive mean matching. We implemented the two-level grid protocol described in Methods (Missing Data): across the 9,648-cell participant × wave grid, 3,355 cells (34.8%) had no observed SWEMWBS (Table 7), and m = 100 imputed datasets were generated. The pilot fractions of missing information for the H1 coefficients were 0.34 (within-person) and 0.81 (between-person): the between-person coefficient depends on person means that are genuinely uncertain for participants with few observed waves, and Rubin’s rules propagate that uncertainty into the pooled intervals. Von Hippel’s rule would require 134 imputations for a 5%-stable standard error; with m = 100 the achieved coefficient of variation of the pooled standard errors is approximately 0.06, which widens the pooled intervals slightly but does not affect the H1 verdicts.

Table 8 compares complete-case and pooled imputed results. The H1 conclusions were unchanged: both pooled 90% confidence intervals fell entirely within ±0.06, so under the preregistered grid neither coefficient showed a practically significant association on the imputed data. The between-person interval widened under imputation, reflecting that person-mean wellbeing is uncertain for participants with few observed waves.

For H2, the comparison separates the preregistered test from the size of the genre differences. As reported in the Results, the complete-case joint Wald test rejected exact equality of the 14 within-person genre coefficients (χ²(13) = 25.1, p = 0.023); under the preregistered decision rule this reading is limited to “at least one pair of genres differs”, with no pairwise interpretation absent formal post-hoc tests. The SD of the 14 coefficient estimates, which describes the size of the differences and includes their estimation error, was 0.022 (complete-case) and 0.027 (imputed). On the imputed data the pooled D_1 tests rejected neither dimension (within: p = 0.838; between: p = 0.512), though these tests carried reduced power at this level of missing information (relative increase in variance 0.64 for the within-person constraints). Distributional diagnostics for the imputation are shown in Figure 7. In sum, accounting for wave nonresponse left the H1 conclusion intact, as neither total-playtime coefficient was practically significant, whereas whether the within-person joint test detected genre differences depended on the frame.

Distributional Diagnostics

The central plausibility check for the imputation model is distributional: imputed wellbeing values should occupy the same range as the observed data and differ from it only in ways explicable by which participants are missing, not by model artefacts.

Figure 7 shows the imputed values to be distributionally almost indistinguishable from the observed data: pooled across all 100 imputations, the imputed values had mean 0.007 and SD 0.74 on the centred scale, against an observed mean of 0 (by construction) and SD of 0.75. The imputation model neither compressed the outcome’s variance nor shifted nonresponders’ imputed wellbeing to implausible regions of the scale. Convergence traces and strip plots are produced alongside the cached imputation (output/qc_imputation/).

Predictive Model Comparison

A complementary way to ask whether genre matters is through predictive performance: does adding genre-specific terms to the total-playtime-only M1 baseline improve out-of-sample prediction? We assessed this using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (Vehtari et al., 2017). A positive difference in expected log predictive density (ELPD) relative to M1 indicates that genre terms help.

M1, the model with total playtime only, showed the highest expected log predictive density, and all three genre specifications predicted slightly worse out-of-sample (Table 9), with ELPD deficits between one and roughly two standard errors of the difference. Adding genre information, in any of the three specifications, therefore did not improve the prediction of wellbeing over total playtime alone. Pareto-k diagnostics flagged 3.8–4% of observations per model (k > 0.7; 239–254 observations), so the ELPD values are approximate; this affects the precision of the differences, not the ordering.

Daily-Timescale Analysis: Design Details and Sensitivity Analyses

Local time was taken from each participant’s reported timezone; Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps (8% of sessions) had their minutes spread uniformly over the recorded day. Exclusions from the analysed daily sample were dominated by days without telemetry coverage; excluded responses entered an all-responses sensitivity refit that retains every response and scores unobserved play as zero. Between-person terms are habitual full-day hours, a participant’s total telemetry over their observed diary period divided by days. The SESOI for the slider and the choice of its minimally important difference are described in Methods (Daily Timescale).

Four sensitivity refits accompany the exploratory daily analysis. Allowing first-order autocorrelated residuals with a within-person day trend (estimated AR(1) = 0.32) widened the within-person interval past zero (β = 0.13, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.29]), as did adjusting for window length (β = 0.15, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.34]). Excluding the 8% of Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps, whose start times were floored to midnight and whose minutes were spread uniformly over the recorded day, left the within-person interval above zero (β = 0.18, 95% CI [0, 0.36]). The all-responses refit, which retains every diary response and scores unobserved play as zero, gave the same between-person lean as the analysed sample (β = -0.37, 95% CI [-1.11, 0.3]). One qualification applies to the daily genre-level intervals: they inherit the exchangeable-residual assumption that the autocorrelation refit relaxes for the total-playtime model only. Like M3, the daily hierarchical-prior model was estimated in non-centred form; with the same sampler settings as M3 it produced no divergent transitions, against 29 in the centred form at the stricter adapt_delta of 0.9995.

Appendix F: Model Specifications and Priors

This appendix gives the equations and priors of the four biweekly models; the Methods describe what each model estimates and why we fitted it (Preregistered Models and Exploratory Models). The daily refits M1-D to M4-D use the same specifications with the daily outcome and exposures; brms then sets the intercept location and the standard-deviation scales from the life-satisfaction outcome (Methods, Daily Timescale).

M1 specification: Total Playtime

M1, the preregistered model for H1, regresses SWEMWBS on the within-person and between-person parts of total playtime, with a random intercept and a random within-person playtime slope for each participant.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= (\alpha + u_{0j}) + (\beta_W + u_{1j})\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} \\ \begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{u0}^2 & \rho_u\, \sigma_{u0}\, \sigma_{u1} \\ \rho_u\, \sigma_{u0}\, \sigma_{u1} & \sigma_{u1}^2 \end{pmatrix} \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, \tilde{y}, 2.5) \\ \beta_W, \beta_B &\propto 1 \end{aligned}

In this and the following equations, i indexes biweekly survey waves, j participants, and, from M2 onwards, g genres. \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} is participant j’s average daily playtime on Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam (hours per day over the 14 days before wave i’s scheduled survey) minus that participant’s mean across all of their survey waves, and \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} is that mean; the mean also covers the 35 waves with an incomplete SWEMWBS, which do not enter the models. \alpha, \beta_W, and \beta_B are the population intercept and slopes; u_{0j} and u_{1j} are participant j’s deviations from \alpha and \beta_W, so that participant j’s own intercept is \alpha + u_{0j} and own within-person slope is \beta_W + u_{1j}; \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u is the covariance matrix of these deviations, with standard deviations \sigma_{u0} and \sigma_{u1} and correlation \rho_u; \sigma is the residual standard deviation; \tilde{y} is the sample median of SWEMWBS; and \propto 1 denotes an improper flat prior.

M2 specification: Independent Genre Coefficients

M2, the preregistered model for H2, replaces total playtime with the within-person and between-person exposures to each of the 14 genres, estimates their coefficients independently, and has a random intercept only.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= (\alpha + u_{0j}) + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) \\ u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_{u0}) \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, \tilde{y}, 2.5) \\ \beta_{W,g}, \beta_{B,g} &\propto 1 \end{aligned}

Here g indexes the G = 14 genres. \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} and \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j} split participant j’s exposure to genre g, the average daily hours spent on games carrying that genre label (a multi-genre game’s full playtime counts towards each of its labels), in the same way as total playtime; \beta_{W,g} and \beta_{B,g} are their coefficients; and \sigma_{u0} is the standard deviation of the participant intercept deviations u_{0j}.

M3 specification: Hierarchical Prior

M3, an exploratory model, keeps M2’s predictors and random intercept but draws the within-person and the between-person genre coefficients from two normal distributions whose centres and standard deviations it estimates.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= (\alpha + u_{0j}) + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) \\ u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_{u0}) \\ \beta_{W,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(\gamma_W, \tau_{\text{within}}) \\ \beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(\gamma_B, \tau_{\text{between}}) \\ \gamma_W, \gamma_B &\propto 1 \\ \tau_{\text{within}}, \tau_{\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Student-}t(3, 0, 2.5) \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, \tilde{y}, 2.5) \end{aligned}

The symbols are as in M2. \gamma_W and \gamma_B are the centres and \tau_{\text{within}} and \tau_{\text{between}} the standard deviations of the distributions from which the within-person and between-person genre coefficients are drawn. \gamma_W and \gamma_B receive the same improper flat prior as the slopes in M1 and M2, and \tau_{\text{within}} and \tau_{\text{between}} describe the size of the genre differences in the within-person (H2a) and between-person (H2b) dimensions. Because the centred form of this model, in which the sampler draws each genre coefficient directly from its normal distribution, produced 68 divergent transitions, we estimate it in the equivalent non-centred form \beta_{W,g} = \gamma_W + \tau_{\text{within}}\, z_{W,g} and \beta_{B,g} = \gamma_B + \tau_{\text{between}}\, z_{B,g}, with z_{W,g}, z_{B,g} \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1). In brms this is a model with slopes \gamma_W and \gamma_B on the summed genre exposures plus two genre-level random terms weighted by the genre exposures (the multi-membership construction that M4 also uses); it changes neither the likelihood nor the priors on \gamma and \tau.

M4 specification: Multi-Membership

M4, an exploratory model, keeps M1’s total-playtime terms and participant effects and lets the genre composition of each wave adjust the within-person and between-person playtime slopes. Formally, this is a multi-membership structure: every wave belongs to all 14 genres, and only the membership weights vary, each equal to the genre’s share of the wave’s summed genre exposure.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= (\alpha + u_{0j}) + \Bigl(\beta_W + u_{1j} + \sum_{g=1}^{G} w_{g,ij}\, s_{W,g}\Bigr) \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\ &\quad + \Bigl(\beta_B + \sum_{g=1}^{G} w_{g,ij}\, s_{B,g}\Bigr) \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} \\ \begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\right) \\ \begin{pmatrix} s_{W,g} \\ s_{B,g} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s\right) \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s &= \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{s,W}^2 & \rho_s\, \sigma_{s,W}\, \sigma_{s,B} \\ \rho_s\, \sigma_{s,W}\, \sigma_{s,B} & \sigma_{s,B}^2 \end{pmatrix} \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, \tilde{y}, 2.5) \\ \beta_W, \beta_B &\propto 1 \\ \sigma_{s,\text{within}}, \sigma_{s,\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Student-}t(3, 0, 2.5) \\ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho_s \\ \rho_s & 1 \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{LKJ}(1) \end{aligned}

The participant terms are as in M1. w_{g,ij} is genre g’s exposure hours in participant j’s wave i divided by the summed exposure hours of all G genres in that wave, so a wave’s weights sum to one; because exposure uses full attribution, a game with two genre labels adds its hours to both. Waves without genre-labelled play, most of them without any recorded play, receive w_{g,ij} = 1/G. s_{W,g} and s_{B,g} are genre g’s adjustments to the within-person and between-person playtime slopes; because the weights describe each wave’s genre mix, the between-person adjustment follows the wave’s mix rather than the participant’s habitual mix. The two adjustments are drawn jointly, with standard deviations \sigma_{s,\text{within}} and \sigma_{s,\text{between}} (written \sigma_{s,W} and \sigma_{s,B} in the equation) and correlation \rho_s; the LKJ(1) prior on their 2 × 2 correlation matrix is uniform over \rho_s.

Because this use of multi-membership is unconventional, we validated the specification by parameter recovery. The simulation fits the manuscript’s own M4 code, read from this document at run time, to 20 synthetic datasets of 200 participants over six waves with known within-person and between-person genre heterogeneity. The 95% credible intervals covered each of the ten true values in at least 19 of the 20 replications, with no divergent transitions. At this sample size, a fraction of the real one, the genre-level standard deviations were estimated with upward bias (posterior means of 0.09 within and 0.07 between persons for true values of 0.04), and the correlation between the within-person and between-person adjustments was weakly identified (true value 0.3, averaged 95% CI [-0.95, 0.93]), so σs should be read with its interval rather than its point estimate (simulation report in the supplementary materials).

Priors

All models use the brms default priors (Bürkner, 2017). The slopes have improper flat priors, so that the data alone determine their estimates, which are directly comparable with the preregistered maximum-likelihood analysis; the exception is M3, whose genre coefficients receive the hierarchical prior that defines the model. brms places the intercept prior on the intercept with all predictors at their sample means, that is, on expected wellbeing at average playtime (for M3, at the mean summed genre exposure), from which brms recovers \alpha after sampling; this prior is Student-t(3, 3.3, 2.5), centred at the sample median of SWEMWBS. The residual standard deviation \sigma and every other standard deviation, including the participant-level standard deviations and the genre-level spreads τ (M3) and σs (M4), have half-Student-t(3, 0, 2.5) priors; their scale is the larger of 2.5 and the median absolute deviation of the outcome, which for SWEMWBS gives 2.5. Both τ and σs are standard deviations of brms group-level terms (for τ, in the non-centred form of M3 described above), so brms assigns this prior to them by default. Each correlation matrix has an LKJ(1) prior, which for a 2 × 2 matrix is uniform over the single correlation. An earlier version used weakly informative Student-t priors on the slopes and intercept, a Half-Normal(0, 0.1) hyperprior on τ and a Normal(0, 0.3) prior on σs; following co-author review, and after those results were known, we adopted the defaults so that no analyst-chosen scale enters the models.
